value.lead: A framework for running any medical practice as a business. It is organized by what has to be managed, not by one vendor's product list: **13 domains**, each broken into areas with what good looks like, where it usually breaks, what to do, and what to measure.
how_to_use: Pick a domain. Each one opens into its areas.
In an area, read *What good looks like* against your own practice, then the questions. Honest answers are the assessment.
Use *What to measure* for the definition, the formula and a benchmark. Where no reliable public benchmark exists, the page says so instead of inventing one.
Open **My practice** to see every area already judged for this practice, with its numbers, risks and next steps.
value.method: The domain list follows the recognized bodies of knowledge for practice management (the MGMA Body of Knowledge, HFMA MAP Keys, the OIG compliance program guidance, the NCQA medical-home concepts and the Medicare quality program) and was checked against the 60 documents of a purchased vendor library. Rules are cited to the regulation or CMS manual. Benchmarks are cited to their source with the data year, and labelled when they are convention and not measurement.

value.lead: The universal framework applied to this practice, using its own financial statements, billing data and public Medicare data. **The practice is profitable and its billing machinery is fast, though two faults were found in it on November 10, 2026. Its main problems are untested billing patterns, coverage and enrollment gaps, a cut from Medicare's quality program that is already set for 2027 and grows in 2028 unless 2026 is reported, and dependence on one physician.**
headline: **Profitable and lean.** $585,057 before owner pay on $1,058,153 of revenue in the last twelve months. Operating cost is 44.7% of revenue.

**Worth about $300,000 today** as a business (range about $50,000 to $680,000). Buyers pay for the profit left after a physician is paid a market wage for this workload. That profit is about $88,000 a year. This is a planning estimate. It depends most on that wage and on how the billing reviews come out.

**The largest money on the table is place of service, and the owner's rule for it is live.** Until November 10, 2026 every care-management line in the five nursing buildings went out as a skilled stay. For long-term residents the correct code pays more in 2026: Medicare allows $142.98 against $80.71 for the first hour of complex care management. Since November 10 billing enters these lines under the long-term code, except in a month when the chart looks skilled (about one resident in eight in October). Care management is billed at month end, so November's lines will be the first to carry it, and whether the billing system keeps the new code has not been checked yet. That is worth an estimated $50,000 to $70,000 a year of Medicare payment. Each facility's list of residents in a Medicare Part A stay is still the proof.

**Two billing patterns still need a chart review before anyone else asks:** visit levels far above national patterns, and advance care planning billed with no tested record of time. A third needs the owner's decision: the charge import, which enters the clinicians' daily charge feed into the billing system, entered 149 October visits (167 charge lines) under the other clinician. On November 10, 2026 the owner decided the 15 lines not yet billed: the 2 initial visits (4 lines) stay under the physician and were saved for billing on November 11, and the 10 other visits (11 lines) still wait for the move to the nurse practitioner; the 152 lines already billed (19 of them paid) still wait for his decision. New claims follow the owner's rules of November 10, 2026: place of service as above, and every initial nursing facility visit under the physician, which is right only when he personally does the visit. On those two points past claims are not being reopened.

**Money is leaking before and after the claim goes out.** On November 10, 2026, 122 visits from the charge feed had no claim: $26,373 of charges, which is not a forecast of payment. 84 of them ($18,802) could never bill because of a software fault found and proven that day. The fix went live on November 11, 2026 (01:20 UTC; the evening of November 10, Eastern time). That day the billing routine saved one test visit and then 51 more, on the terms the owner approved; all 52 read back correctly, and none is confirmed billed yet. 50 of them wait for the claim run; the billing system's claim check holds the other 2 for missing data, which a billing chat session or the owner clears. The other 32 wait: 10 for the clinician move, and 22 for the owner (an admission-date question on 15; a coverage check dated to the visit that did not confirm the plan on 7). A guard for the save step went live later that afternoon (19:45 UTC), after the 52 saves. 30% of recent claim lines paid nothing, and two thirds of those carry one denial code, the one Medicare gives most often on care-management lines. $342,620 is open with 35% older than 90 days.

**First moves for the owner, in date order.** Due November 10 and not recorded as done: replace the database access key that was shared in a chat. November 11: turn off open sign-up to the practice's web application. November 12: pause the automatic write-off of old balances; call about one health plan's network removal notice. November 13: file the physician's Medicaid renewal, after resetting the Medicaid portal password (December 1 is the last call; the agreement expires December 27, 2026). Also November 13: mark which of the October visits entered under the other clinician were the physician's own, and decide on the rest this week. This week too: answer billing's questions on the 22 never-billed visits that wait for him (which admission date is right on 15; which plan to bill on the 7 the coverage check did not confirm). November 17: engage a healthcare attorney before the visit-level audit starts; answer billing's three questions about the place-of-service rule. November 18: close the open items on the hospital reappointment (the hospital is 37.8% of charges). November 19: ask each nursing facility for its list of residents in a Medicare Part A stay. No date: accept the look-up vendor's invitation, which only he can, and decide whether to take the call she asked for. The work list has 11 more items for the owner due by November 25.

**Medicare's quality program: an estimated cut of about 9% of 2028 Medicare payments is at stake.** November 30: last day to change the registration; the program's service center can say whether the option chosen fits a nursing-facility practice. December 15: name the one improvement activity both clinicians already carried out for 90 days in a row in 2026. December 21 (calendar entry; the limit is January 1): renew for 2027 the rule that adds the advance care plan code to Medicare claims, because billing adds it only to visits dated in 2026. December 31: last visit date for that code to count toward the 2028 payment; the first three lines were entered on November 11 and taken off again about two minutes later, when the billing system's claim check held the three visits for a no-charge line, so no coded line stands yet; under billing's rule the next lines go in at one cent. January 4 to March 31, 2027: attest the activity.

**Other dates.** Salary and owner-loan decisions with the accountant are needed before December 31; the work list dates them December 18. Medicare claims that were never accepted expire one year after the date of service, so some from late 2025 expire each week.

value.lead: Patterns in the practice's own billing data that an auditor's software would also see, set beside the rule each one touches. **A pattern is a reason to look at charts. It is not a finding that anything was billed wrongly.**
how_to_use: Read the findings in order. Critical and high come first.

Engage a healthcare attorney first, so that the reviews of past visit claims are directed by counsel. Place of service on new claims follows the owner's rule since November 10, 2026; get each facility's list of residents in a Medicare Part A stay to back it. Do not move visit levels up or down to match national averages. The note for that day decides the level.

The billing database holds claims, not clinical notes. The findings on billing patterns still have to be tested against the charts: who saw each patient on the October visits entered under the other clinician, which the owner marks this week, and visit levels and advance care planning, in the audit the attorney directs. Place of service has to be tested against each facility's list of residents in a Medicare Part A stay, which the practice still has to get; the 84 never-billed visits are a software fault proven from the billing records. The last finding, on care-management claims, is not up for review. The owner confirmed on November 10, 2026 that consent, care plans and time records are on file for these claims.

When a review that the attorney directs is finished, its result goes to the attorney, not into this application. On the work list record only that the step is complete, and the date. For the other reviews, record the result and the date on the work list.
value.foot: Management information and education, not legal or coding advice. If a chart review shows Medicare was overpaid, federal law requires reporting and returning the money within 60 days of identifying it. A prompt, good-faith review of related claims pauses those 60 days, for no more than 180 days after the first overpayment was identified.

value.lead: The purchased CleanClaimRx library and every issue of the vendor's free newsletter, read in full and scored. It was used as an outline to make sure the universal framework misses nothing, and every rule or number it states was treated as unverified until found in a primary source.
verdict: **60 documents, 2,566 pages, list price $1,032 for the bundles bought.** Every document was written by an AI system with no named author, sources or dates on its numbers.
**Quality, scored 1 to 5 after reading each document in full:** 1 scored 1, 29 scored 2, 30 scored 3. None scored 4 or 5.
**Best use:** as a checklist of topics and worksheets. The operating routines (daily queues, root-cause logs, reconciliation steps) are sound and transfer to any practice.
**Do not rely on it for rules or numbers.** Benchmarks are unsourced, several code and deadline statements are wrong, and almost nothing addresses Medicare facility-based billing.
**All 445 rules and numbers extracted from the documents were checked against primary sources.** 212 partly, 94 contradicted, 74 supported, 44 unverifiable, 21 outdated.

**The vendor's free newsletter was read too: 21 issues published from May to November 2026.** Quality: 11 scored 2, 10 scored 3. Of 105 news claims checked against the original announcement or rule: 29 supported, 55 partly, 8 contradicted, 3 outdated, 10 unverifiable. It is where the vendor reports dated news (new rules, deadlines, payer announcements), which the purchased documents lack. Each item is checked in the table below.
